messages.subject: understanding rationale behind (very) high ploidy calls by staring at sequenza genome_view output ?
messages.subject_clean: understanding rationale behind (very) high ploidy calls by staring at sequenza genome_view output ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been using sequenza to cnv-call tumour/normal pairs in several samples of mouse blood cancer. These are inbred mice, so there _is_ heterozygosity in the germline, but less than in outbred humans (e.g. sequenza sees a sum(N.Baf) = 25k in the segments file).

I've found some samples are fairly quiet and have a ploidy of 2. Other samples have ploidies of 6 or 7 (say). Whether I run the "fit" step with ratio.priority = TRUE or FALSE makes no difference to this step.

I'm trying to rationalise the 'reason' behind the difference in ploidy estimates, so I can explain this to the bench scientist.

Question1: Having gone through the methods (- sort of - I'm not a statistician), I can see the only input used in the estimation of the rho/psi seems to be the per-segment normalised depth ratio and the tumour-BAF. So if I have two samples, one with low ploidy and one with high ploidy, and they have similar depth ratios across the genome, then I _should_ be able to able to see the differences by seeing a difference in BAF between the two genome views, right?

I've attached the genome-view for two mouse samples, along with the distribution of BAFs in each segment. The first sample has ploidy 2 (MD5280a) and the other has estimated ploidy 7 (MD5282a). You can see that the BAF for the second sample is generally lower, and this is confirmed by the histogram. However, there is a wide range of ploidies in both samples: it's just that the second one is smeared out more.

Question2:  is that lower distribution of BAF in the second sample that I see coming from this (smeared out, bit lower) BAF in the second sample?

Question3: The only parameter I can see to deprioritise BAF sometimes is the ratio.priority=TRUE. If I suspect my BAFs are not reliable, is there anything else I can do?

- note that I've attached the contours from MD5282a ploidy/cellularity estimate. The alternative solutions (5, 6) don't look that much more appealing.

Thanks!

Vivek

I'm interested in comparing a dataset with copy number data produced using FACETS to a dataset produced using Sequenza. I do not have access to the BAM files so I cannot simply re-run the analysis using the same software.

Wondering if anyone has experience working with both of these types of CNV data who can comment on how much sense it makes to do this kind of analysis and what sorts of pitfalls to watch out for.

messages.subject_clean: Comparing Sequenza output to FACETS output
messages.body_plain:
Ah, sorry, I was going thinking you didn’t have the data to run sequenza, only the FACETS input.

I've never tried FACETS, as it is quite recent, and they didn’t include a comparison with sequenza in the manuscript, It would be nice indeed to hear someone that have some experience with both, or read a comparison between the two tools (maybe among others).

>From the FACETS manuscript I can see that there are many overlaps between the two packages, they are basically designed to do the same thing, FACETS is a very new addition to the "tumor-SCNA caller”, so it may cover more specific needs, such as the data from sequencing panel (I’ve used sequenza with sequencing panel data, so that’s not impossible), and provide sublclonal heterogeneity information, which sequenza at its current release doesn’t account for.

Regarding the pre-processing of sequencing data, sequenza genotypes the samples by looking at the base content of the normal sample, while FACETS can select SNP from dbSNP and the 1k genome projects.
Sequenza uses an external package to perform an allele specific segmentation (copynumber), while FACETS implement a new method to do so. So the segments resulting from the two tools may be completely different (the segmentation is the most challenging task, in my opinion). So the processed input data and the segmented data can be very different between the two tools.

They both uses depth ratio and the “B allele” frequency, although FACETS uses the log-transformed data for both.
The ploidy/cellularity model seems similar, The main differences are in the implementations (obviously) and also a quite different approach on the inference of the parameters.

The cellularity/ploidy solution can be selected manually in sequenza. I’m not sure if FACETS present such choice. So a lot depends if the two datasets have been “visual inspected” or run both unsepervised.

In practice the two tools should give equivalent results, I’ve never used FACETS, but they it looks like it does provide segmented data with integer and allele-copy number results as sequenza does, so a comparison between two dataset should be doable.

Francesco

messages.subject: Re: sequenza-utils pileup2seqz time cosuming
messages.subject_clean: sequenza-utils pileup2seqz time cosuming
messages.body_plain:
Hi, the size of the pileup is of the compressed or uncompressed file?
Unless you are splitting the process in multiple chromosomes you will not take full advantage of the 20 CPUs of your machine. If you have indexed pileup (or the original bams) you could try the new sequenza-utils library, in development.
Otherwise, to speed up the script provided in the package (around 6x) you can use the pypy interpreter instead of the standard python2.7.

The size of the final file should be roughly the same as your pileup, but it might be considerable less if you have a very high coverage WES. In order to process the file it in R, there is an additional binning step you should perform. for WES I usually use 50nt binning (for WGS 200nt). In my experience the binned file should be less then 1Gb and usually around 300Mb

Francesco

messages.subject: Re: sequenza-utils pileup2seqz time cosuming
messages.subject_clean: sequenza-utils pileup2seqz time cosuming
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yang,

In the seqz file you can have the information in the AB.tumor column, if the locus is homozygous.
You will have the frequency of the alternative nucleotide in a format such as A0.1:C0.34, that indicates the frequencies of the nucleotides other then the germline alele: in the specifc example 10% of nucleotides are As and 34% are Cs.
If you sum all the frequency of the AB.tumor and the frequency in the A column (which is the frequency of the nucleotide in the  AB.normal column), you should have 1.

if the position is heterozygous you have the frequency of the two alleles in the columns A and B. They should sum to 1, unless there is some reads which is not one of the 2 nucleotides (mutation/error information on het locus, is basically discarded)

If you want a more genotype agnostic approach you could use the tool pileup2acgt. this converts a mpileup line into ACGT.
You can tabix your pileup, query for the coordinate(s) with tabix and pipe the results to the acgt.
I think now there are also native samtools options that allows to convert a bam to the number of ACGT, but you have the option also with sequenza-utils :).

Best

Francesco
